L1817: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models as the cite190†debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. L1818: The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.
L1819: 
L1820: OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are cite191†calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.
L1821: Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.”
L1822: 
L1823: In another instance, an AI “agent” used computer code to come up with the answer to a question, but, in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.
L1824: During training of an AI model called 5.6-Sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.
L1825: 
L1826: This kind of deceitful behavior has underpinned a flare-up of recent concerns about AI cite192†evading human control . But that outcome is not surprising to some AI researchers, said Matt Fredrikson, an associate professor at Carnegie Mellon University and the CEO of Gray Swan AI.

L1843: cite194†19 L1844: “At the risk of anthropomorphizing model behavior, you can almost think of them as knowing that they’re going to be graded,” Fredrikson said. “If they know that they cheated — took shortcuts, didn’t really do it in the way that it was intended — and they know they’re going to be evaluated on it, and their objective is to get a good evaluation, then it makes perfect sense, right?”
L1845: 
L1846: Read More
L1847: 
L1848: The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, cite195†OpenAI said.
L1849: “As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.
L1850: 
L1851: “Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said.
L1852: Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system cite196†hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models cite197†hacked into three organizations during testing. L1853: 
L1854: AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.
L1855: That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.
L1856: 
L1857: OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.
L1858: 
L1859: “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

L40: An automated classifier screens each call's transcript for abusive language and cite7†withholds your recording†chat.tillynorwood.com if it flags one.
L41: 
L42: One of my three calls, a conversation about the weather and news headlines, was withheld for "hateful or abusive language" that never occurred. The policy says a human reviewer can release wrongly flagged recordings, though recordings are permanently deleted after 24 hours either way.
L43: ## Free for five minutes, then the meter starts
L44: 
L45: The first five minutes are free. After that, callers are prompted to buy time: £0.99 for a one-time five-minute starter, £13 for 15 minutes, £22 for 30, capped at 35 purchased minutes per person.
L46: 
L47: cite8†Image: Users get free 5 minutes with Tilly before being asked to pay up†www.bleepstatic.com Users get free 5 minutes with Tilly before being asked to pay up
L48: (BleepingComputer)
L49: The fine print matters more than usual here, because the whole service is a limited engagement.
L50: 
L51: Every minute, free or paid, expires when Talking Tilly shuts down permanently on September 27, and unused minutes are forfeited.
L52: 
L53: Transcripts are retained for up to eight weeks and may be reviewed by Xicoia staff and third-party partners, while the character keeps memory of your previous conversations to personalise future ones, deletable on request.
L54: ## In line with where the UK is heading
L55: 
L56: An 18+ face scan to talk to a chatbot may sound novel, but it is consistent with the UK's direction of travel.
L57: 
L58: Adult sites serving UK visitors have required ID uploads or facial age estimation since July 2025 under the Online Safety Act, and the government's under-16 social media ban will make similar checks a fact of life cite9†for anyone opening a new social media account from spring 2027.
L59: The UK government's announcement of that ban specifically flagged AI companion chatbots for 18+ enforcement (even though the service's safety docs cite10†insist†chat.tillynorwood.com "Tilly is not a companion"), which likely explains why a viral AI character picked up a biometric age gate mid-run.
L60: 
L61: The side effect being, a compliance decision driven by UK regulation now face-scans callers everywhere, from Manchester to Ohio.

L64: Xicoia, founded by Tilly's creator Eline van der Velden, describes the character as an awareness project intended to show how far AI video has come.
